verify.inputs_review:
Limits of this check: I could not open any web source. This turn's web-search budget was already used up, and cov.com, flightglobal.com and chrobinson.com did not resolve, so I stopped trying other hosts as the tool asked. The checks rest on S&P Capital IQ Embraer call transcripts (2011 to 8 May 2026) and a Capital IQ financials file, both in the repo. Every basis item dated after May 2026 is unverified: S301-2/3/4, SEC232-1, DIP-2/3, ELE-*, SAN-4, KOR-1, the finalization in KOR-3, and TAR-5. The ranges should hold up if any of them turns out wrong.

P_us_formal_action (0.3/0.5/0.75): defensible. The best evidence is new: Embraer said it was 'the only manufacturer to pay tariffs on aircraft exports' from April 2025 to February 2026, because EU, UK and Japan deals brought aircraft back to 0% and Brazil got none. The US has therefore already treated Brazilian aircraft worse than Airbus's. Over a 10-13 year window, with Boeing able to petition, 0.5 is reasonable, and the high could go to 0.8.

P_us_sustained_ge10pct (0.1/0.22/0.4): restate the basis. The US airline importer paid the duty, and only on the non-US content (CFO: 'we always deduct the U.S. [content]'; E175 effective rate 'lower than 10%'). At 40% or more US content, a 10% headline rate is about 6% of the price or less. Say whether the threshold is the headline or the effective rate. If effective, a base of about 0.15 fits better. The 10-month episode was ended by a court ruling, not by a policy choice, so it is weak evidence of low political will to tax.

P_us_market_effectively_blocked (0.03/0.08/0.2): fine. The Bombardier figures were not verified here but agree with the well-known record.

US_tariff_rate_if_taxed (10/25/50): fine as headline rates, but apply them as effective = headline x (1 - US content share). With more than 40% US content today, and possibly more if the engines are US-sourced, a 25% headline is about 15% of the price or less. The 2026 rates of 25% and 12.5% are unverified.

P_embraer_korea_builds_US_final_assembly (0.2/0.4/0.6): the evidence is better than 'judgement'. Embraer offers local final assembly when an order is large: the KC-390 'will be assembled and produced in the U.S.' if the USAF orders enough, and India's MTA requires local assembly. US-4's 'refused US E2 assembly' overstates; the CEO said 'other changes in the footprint, yes, we are making studies'. A base of 0.45-0.5 is defensible. Keep the low at 0.2 for the golden share and Brazilian industrial policy.

world_single_aisle_share_ex_China_ex_US (0.55/0.60/0.63): the arithmetic is fine. It mixes the 2024 China and 2025 global outlooks and uses North America as a stand-in for the US, which slightly understates the ex-US share. Keep it.

politically_accessible_fraction (0.85/0.95/1.0): a high of 1.0 contradicts the basis, which itself lists haircuts (Korean Air's Boeing order, Gulf deals tied to US trade). Suggest 0.75/0.88/0.95. India and Turkey asking for local work share is access with conditions, not a closed market.

addressable_world_share_if_US_open (0.75/0.8/0.83): consistent with China at about 20%. Fine.

embraer_korea_capture_share (0.03/0.08/0.15): check the scale. 33,285 jets over 20 years is about 1,660 single-aisle deliveries a year. About 60% of that is ex-US and ex-China, or about 1,000 a year. 8% of that is about 80 a year (6.7 a month), which equals Embraer's entire 2025 commercial output of 78 jets. That is plausible only for a mature programme with a strong partner. It also conflicts with the game's generic entrant at 20 a month (240 a year, about 24% of the same pool): make sure the two entrant settings do not double count. Suggest a base of 0.05-0.06 and a high of 0.12.

BNDES_annual_Embraer_financing (7/9.6/12 BRL bn): the arithmetic is right (28.8/3), but LEV-3 is unverified, and the 169 aircraft look like approvals covering later deliveries, not a yearly rate. At the CEO's own conversion (BRL 20bn, 'close to $4 billion'), BRL 9.6bn is about US$1.9bn, or about 35 narrowbodies at US$55M. BNDES alone could finance only part of an 80-a-year programme. Treat this input as approval capacity, not disbursement.

embraer_north_america_revenue_share (0.55/0.587/0.6): the 2025 figure is confirmed (58.6% in the Capital IQ BRL data against 58.7% claimed). The same data gives 59.5% for 2024 against the 59.1% claimed, which is probably currency translation and does not matter here. North America is not the same as the US. The range is fine.

findings.claim: Irwin and Pavcnik estimate that the 1992 US-EU civil aircraft agreement raised Airbus and Boeing prices by about 3.7%, consistent with a roughly 5% rise in marginal cost.
findings.detail: Structural differentiated-products demand (Berry 1994 / nested logit), aircraft prices, sales and characteristics 1969-1998. The search summary says the 3.7% applies to both narrow- and wide-body markets. Read as roughly 0.74 pass-through of a common cost shock under duopoly conduct. Full text could not be opened (nber.org is not reachable from WebFetch), so this rests on the abstract and search snippets.
findings.source_title: Airbus versus Boeing Revisited: International Competition in the Aircraft Market (NBER WP 8648; J. Int. Econ. 64(2), 2004)

findings.claim: Irwin and Pavcnik report aircraft price-cost margins (p-c)/p of about 14-17%, with occasional periods when they drop to 3-5%.
findings.detail: Markups are computed for several learning-rate assumptions. For the L-1011 at a 20% learning rate, they estimate margins of -0.19 to 0.2. The snippet does not say whether 14-17% is wide-body only; the paper's demand system is estimated for wide-bodies. Use as an order of magnitude for a duopoly Lerner index.
findings.source_title: Airbus versus Boeing revisited (Dartmouth-hosted copy)

findings.claim: In Irwin and Pavcnik's simulation, a new entrant product (the A380) cuts 747 long-range share by up to 14.8 points, depending on the A380 discount, but hurts Airbus's own A330/A340 even more.
findings.detail: Scenarios price the A380 at list and at 10%, 20% and 30% discounts. One snippet says Boeing prices fall by 0.6 to 2.2%; the scenario behind that range is unconfirmed (low confidence on that sub-figure). Another draft reports only a 1.6-point share decline. Lesson for the model: a new product takes most from its closest substitutes, and the price response of rivals is small, a few percent.
findings.source_title: NBER Working Paper 8648 (PDF)

findings.claim: Benkard's dynamic oligopoly model of wide-bodies explains high concentration and persistent pricing below static marginal cost through learning-by-doing, and finds a concentration restriction would reduce welfare.
findings.detail: Markov-perfect equilibrium with endogenous entry, exit, prices and quantities. The unconstrained equilibrium gives about 10% less welfare than a social planner. Secondary summaries say the estimates imply prices up to 50% below cost when a model is first introduced, and lower still against more experienced rivals. The L-1011 markup over price was essentially zero or negative. Learning is about exhausted by around 80 L-1011s (learning parameter -0.29, about an 18% learning rate). The full PDF on web.stanford.edu could not be fetched.
findings.source_title: Benkard, A Dynamic Analysis of the Market for Wide-Bodied Commercial Aircraft, Review of Economic Studies 71(3)

findings.claim: Neven and Seabright estimate that Airbus's presence cut Boeing's profits by at least $100bn and McDonnell Douglas's by about two-thirds, and that Airbus lowered world welfare (equal weights) while raising European welfare.
findings.detail: Calibrated simulation with three players and four segments, commissioned by the UK DTI. Implication: entry mostly moves profits from incumbents to customers and the entrant, and duplicated fixed costs can outweigh the consumer gains. These are working-paper figures; the published Economic Policy no. 21 version may differ.
findings.source_title: European Industrial Policy: The Airbus Case (working-paper version)

findings.claim: Baldwin and Krugman's Cournot simulation of the A300 versus 767 found that the rest of the world gained from cheaper aircraft after Airbus entered, while the subsidy was usually not welfare-improving for Europe.
findings.detail: The model compares an Airbus monopoly, a duopoly and a Boeing monopoly. Critics note the homogeneous-product Cournot assumption and that McDonnell Douglas is left out. No price-change number was retrievable.
findings.source_title: Korean review of Baldwin-Krugman (and NBER chapter c5847)

findings.claim: Calibrated simulation models of the aircraft industry show 'extreme sensitivity to the impact of two versus three competitors' (Neven and Seabright 1995 against Klepper 1990).
findings.detail: Cited in a Harvard case paper on Airbus and Boeing, probably Esty-Ghemawat. Klepper's 1990 paper on a third entrant (European Economic Review 34(4)) could not be read. Treat the size of the 2-to-3 firm price effect as structurally uncertain, which argues for a wide low/high band.
findings.source_title: Esty - Airbus vs Boeing (Scribd copy)

findings.claim: Reuters sources put Delta's 2016 CS100 discount at close to two-thirds off a $71.8M list price, against a typical discount of roughly half.
findings.detail: Firm order for 75 CS100s, valued by Bombardier at about $5.6bn at list. Estimates ranged from 40-50% (consultant Pierre Jeanniot, via CBC) to 65-70% (Fox Business). Canaccord's David Tyerman questioned how profitable later CSeries orders would be.
findings.source_title: Big Delta order boosts momentum for Bombardier's CSeries jets (Reuters via Investing.com)

findings.claim: Boeing's trade petition said Bombardier sold CS100s to Delta at $19.6M each, against a production cost of $33.2M.
findings.detail: That is about 41% below cost on Boeing's figures (my arithmetic). Bombardier disputed the number. $19.6M is Boeing's figure after ITC-guideline adjustments, so these are claims by an interested party.
findings.source_title: Bombardier-Delta deal can put Boeing out of business, company claims (Leeham)

findings.claim: Bombardier booked a $492M onerous-contract provision for its deeply discounted CSeries deals with Delta, Air Canada and airBaltic (127 aircraft), about $3.9M of expected loss per aircraft.
findings.detail: Non-cash IFRS charge in Q2 2016 (75 for Delta, 45 for Air Canada, 7 for airBaltic). On a net price in the low $20Ms, the loss is roughly 15-20% of price (my arithmetic). This is the entrant's own admission that launch pricing was below cost.
findings.source_title: Bombardier losses on key CSeries sales total $492 million (Aviation Week)

findings.claim: The US Commerce Department's final determination set a 79.82% dumping margin and a 212.39% subsidy rate on Bombardier 100-150 seat aircraft, 292.21% combined.
findings.detail: Under the preliminary rates the combined figure was 299.45%. The dumping margin was based on adverse facts available because Bombardier did not answer the questionnaire, so it is not a measured price-cost gap.
findings.source_title: Commerce fact sheet: dumping and subsidization of 100- to 150-seat large civil aircraft from Canada

findings.claim: The ITC voted 4-0 that Boeing was not injured: it found Boeing lost no sales or revenue, that the CSeries was unlikely to depress US prices, and that Bombardier was unlikely to give other buyers Delta-level discounts.
findings.detail: 194-page opinion. Key points: the 110-seat CS100 and the 737 MAX 7 do not compete, and the Delta discount was treated as a one-off launch-customer price. The duties were never imposed.
findings.source_title: U.S. trade agency rejected CSeries duties as jet sales did not hurt Boeing (Reuters via Yahoo)

findings.claim: To block the CS100 at United in 2016, Boeing sold 65 737-700s at an estimated $20-25M each (about $22M) against an $80.6M list price, roughly 73% off.
findings.detail: 40 ordered in January 2016 and 25 in March. Reuters said United likely paid well below half of list. The ITC staff report said United first sought a smaller aircraft and signed with Boeing only after a 'sweetheart deal'. The 737-700 was an end-of-line, paid-off model. Against a typical ~50% discount (about $40M net), this is roughly a 45% further cut on one contested campaign (my arithmetic).
findings.source_title: Boeing just gave United a massive discount (Business Insider); Leeham 2016-01-21

findings.claim: The ITC staff report found moderate-to-high substitutability between US- and Canadian-made 100-150 seat aircraft and recorded United's 'sweetheart deal' with Boeing.
findings.detail: The staff report makes no recommendations. Evidence that an incumbent cuts prices hard in campaigns where a credible entrant bids, even when the overall market price effect is small.
findings.source_title: US trade staff issue final report before Bombardier vote (FlightGlobal)

findings.claim: Moody's estimated JetBlue paid about $23-28M per A220-300 in 2018, 66-72% below list, in a campaign where the E195-E2 was the main rival.
findings.detail: 60 aircraft, about $5.4bn at list, $1.4-1.7bn estimated actual. Moody's analyst Jonathan Root cited appraisers. Leeham called the E195-E2 the real competitor and the order a blow to Embraer.
findings.source_title: Airbus A220s sold to JetBlue at discount of up to 72%: Moody's (BNN Bloomberg)

findings.claim: Spirit AeroSystems booked $328.8M of extra forward losses on the A220 in 2024, which it tied partly to pricing talks with Airbus, and $242.2M more in the first nine months of 2025.
findings.detail: Shows the A220, priced to compete with the E2 and the smallest A320/737 variants, still loses money across its supply chain years after Airbus took control. These are Spirit's losses, not Airbus's.
findings.source_title: Spirit AeroSystems Form 10-K FY2024

findings.claim: Leeham described Embraer's E2 as squeezed by the Airbus-owned A220, with Embraer Commercial Aviation's CEO John Slattery saying Embraer could not compete against Airbus's marketing might alone.
findings.detail: JetBlue chose the A220-300 over the E195-E2 to replace 60 E190s. Embraer claims the E195-E2 has an 18% lower trip cost than the A320neo.
findings.source_title: The Squeeze on Embraer (Leeham)

findings.claim: Boeing's 2019 10-K says intense pricing pressure is expected to continue or intensify, and points to Airbus's expansion in the 100-150 seat market after it took over the C Series.
findings.detail: An incumbent officially acknowledging price pressure from a third design backed by a strong owner.
findings.source_title: Boeing Form 10-K FY2019

findings.claim: Reuters reported in 2012 that Airbus and Boeing were in their fiercest single-aisle share battle in a decade, with single-aisles offered at discounts of as much as 50% and Airbus's John Leahy saying 'They have started a price war.'
findings.detail: The A320neo/737 MAX launch period, about 4-5 years before entry into service (neo 2016, MAX 2017). Boeing's Randy Tinseth acknowledged pricing was aggressive.
findings.source_title: How plane giants descended into global 'price war' (Reuters via Mail & Guardian)

findings.claim: Wells Fargo estimated Southwest's 737 MAX launch-customer base price at $34.7M, 64% off MAX 8 list, but did not see it as evidence of a price war.
findings.detail: $5.67bn for 131 MAXs delivered 2019-2022, $43.3M each after escalation (9 years at 2.5%). The same piece says Boeing offered the MAX at more than 50% off and Airbus offered up to 60% off on the A320 family. AirInsight estimated about 48% for Southwest. Southwest's 8-K gives about $14bn at list with confidential credits and concessions.
findings.source_title: Wells Fargo estimates Southwest paid base price $34.7m for MAX (Leeham)

findings.claim: UBS analyst David Strauss estimated 737 discounts at about 59% in 2014, up since the MAX launch in 2011, with some deals reaching 65%; 777 discounts were about 54% and 787 about 46%.
findings.detail: If typical discounts went from about 50% to about 59%, net prices fell about 18% (my arithmetic). This is an upper reference for a pure duopoly price war around new-variant launches.
findings.source_title: Odds and Ends: Boeing discounting; A380 analysis; A320neo LEAP (Leeham)

findings.claim: In American Airlines' 2011 split order (260 Airbus, 200 Boeing), Airbus reportedly offered big discounts and about $6bn of preferential financing, and Boeing kept its share by committing to re-engine the 737 (the MAX).
findings.detail: A credible new-technology offer from one maker (the neo) forced the other into a product response plus price. About $22.6bn at list.
findings.source_title: Airbus, Boeing to share American Airlines order (Washington Times)

findings.claim: A blogger's estimate puts Ryanair's 2014 737 MAX 200 net price at about $38.8M, about 69% off a basic price near $102M; Ryanair's filing says only that Boeing gave significant price concessions.
findings.detail: An individual aviation-finance blogger, not a sell-side analyst, with assumptions on capex. Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary said the price was a small premium per seat over the 2013 737-800 deal. 100 firm, 100 options, $11bn at list for the firm aircraft.
findings.source_title: Ryanair's aircraft cost advantage (blog)

findings.claim: Ryanair's O'Leary said in 2021 that playing Boeing against Airbus was 'doomed to failure': 'Basically its a duopoly... You don't get leverage by holding discussions with one or the other.'
findings.detail: Said after 737 MAX 10 talks collapsed over price. With sold-out backlogs, a two-supplier market gives large buyers little leverage, which is the gap a third source would fill.
findings.source_title: Ryanair ready for long wait for Boeing to cut Max price, says O'Leary (Irish Times)

findings.claim: Airbus CEO Guillaume Faury said A320neo-family pricing was 'holding' and 'performing reasonably well', while widebody campaigns faced aggressive pricing from Boeing.
findings.detail: Duopoly single-aisle pricing is firm while backlogs exceed output (over 7,000 A320neo-family jets in backlog). The date is not shown in the search result: it was a February full-year briefing, probably 2024 (inferred).
findings.source_title: Airbus experiencing 'aggressive' pricing in widebody campaigns: Faury (FlightGlobal)

findings.claim: Boeing Commercial Airplanes' 2018 operating margin was 13.0% (9.4% in 2017) on 806 deliveries, its pre-MAX-grounding duopoly peak.
findings.detail: Benchmark for incumbent margins under duopoly with a mature 737 line. Covers all BCA programmes, not single-aisle alone.
findings.source_title: Boeing Reports Record 2018 Results and Provides 2019 Guidance

findings.claim: Airbus commercial aircraft EBIT Adjusted was EUR 5,470M in 2025 (2024: EUR 5,093M) on about EUR 52.6bn of revenue, an implied margin of about 10.4%.
findings.detail: The 10.4% is derived, not published. Group EBIT Adjusted was EUR 7,128M on EUR 73.4bn revenue; 793 deliveries.
findings.source_title: Airbus reports Full-Year (FY) 2025 results

findings.claim: A320neo current market values rose above base values in Q1 2024, after the gap had narrowed since late 2022, which signals firm new-aircraft pricing in a supply-constrained duopoly.
findings.detail: More than 85 lessors held A320neos. A mid-2025 AirInsight/IBA piece put the A321neo market value near $58M (base value $60M) and the MAX 8 near $45M, roughly half of list (low confidence on that secondary figure).
findings.source_title: Acumen market insight (A320neo)

findings.claim: In the Canada-Brazil WTO fight, Brazil's PROEX gave up to a 3.8-point interest rebate over 15 years on 85% of the price; Bombardier said this cut the 50-seat ERJ-145 price by $2.5M against CRJ prices of $17-19M.
findings.detail: About 13-15% of price on contested regional-jet deals (my arithmetic). Bombardier said it could tolerate a gap of about $4M. The 1999 WTO panel ruled PROEX regional-aircraft payments illegal export subsidies, upheld on appeal. Canada later sought sanctions of up to $3.4bn, and a 2002 ruling found some Canadian loans to Bombardier illegal too. Sources differ on whether the $2.5M referred to the ERJ-145 or ERJ-135.
findings.source_title: Regional brinkmanship (FlightGlobal); WTO DS46 panel report

findings.claim: Bombardier's CEO said an Embraer 50-seat offer to a US airline was too low to match and that Bombardier could not sustain that pricing.
findings.detail: Shows entrant (Embraer) price aggression in a two-supplier segment. A Wikipedia-derived figure puts the ERJ-145 at about $15M, about $4M under the CRJ (low confidence, undated). The FlightGlobal article's date was not shown (late 1990s).
findings.source_title: Bombardier is foiled by Embraer 50-seat scoop (FlightGlobal)

findings.claim: Embraer's weak Q4 2014 commercial results were blamed on fierce price competition with Bombardier and big discounts on E1s ahead of the E2.
findings.detail: In a two-supplier regional market, a rival's new model forces discounts on the outgoing model. In its Q4 2022 call, Embraer management said older E175-E1 deals were still weighing on pricing.
findings.source_title: Embraer's Drop Could Be a Buying Opportunity (Motley Fool)

findings.claim: China Eastern's filing gave a C919 list price of $99M and said actual prices are lower; the first production C919 was priced higher than expected.
findings.detail: A Straits Times report via AVweb said China had hoped for about $50M and ended near $100M. The Air China deal priced the C919 at $108M list, both sides agreeing to below-list prices (Caixin via SCMP, described as 2024).
findings.source_title: First production Comac C919 narrowbody completes maiden flight, price higher than expected (CompositesWorld)

findings.claim: China Eastern ordered 100 C919s worth $9.9bn at list ($99M each) with a significant, undisclosed discount.
findings.detail: No source found documents A320neo or 737 MAX price cuts in China caused by the C919. A secondary claim of about a 50% discount for China Eastern is unverified.
findings.source_title: China's Planemaker Gets $9.9 Billion Order for 100 C919 Jets (Bloomberg)

findings.claim: IBA judges the C919 unlikely to reach A320neo or 737 MAX 8 values given limited market penetration; a Cirium projection gives the C919 about 25% of Chinese single-aisle deliveries through 2043 (Boeing 30%, Airbus 45%).
findings.detail: The Cirium split comes via a secondary summary. Implication: a politically allocated entrant takes share in a protected market, at Boeing's expense more than Airbus's, without visibly cutting Western prices. Date not shown in the search result.
findings.source_title: Comac's rising impact in China's aviation market (IBA)

findings.claim: In an Aviation Week/Bank of America survey of 492 respondents (45% airlines), 71% said they would still choose an Embraer narrowbody if convinced of its merits, even if Boeing and Airbus launched new aircraft at about the same time; only 5% of airlines disagreed.
findings.detail: Secondhand figures from the same survey: 47% want 150-179 seats, 26% 180-189, 18% 190-229. The date is not shown: probably November 2021, inferred from an Informa Dubai Airshow 2021 / AW&ST editors' picks listing.
findings.source_title: Aviation Week/BofA Survey Shows Great Interest In Potential Embraer Narrowbody

findings.claim: United CEO Scott Kirby said at IATA in June 2024 'we need more competition in the aerospace business', named Embraer as a possible new major player and called COMAC unlikely.
findings.detail: Kirby argued Boeing had little incentive in a duopoly to spend $10bn on a new airplane. A later report (aviationa2z, 2026-10-31, lower-tier source) quotes Kirby: 'We need a third aircraft manufacturer, to be blunt.'
findings.source_title: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby wants more competition in aerospace (Fortune)

findings.claim: Embraer's CEO Francisco Gomes Neto said the narrowbody segment could support 'three or four' makers, but ruled out a near-term 737/A320 rival; any move is unlikely before the next decade.
findings.detail: Airbus CEO Faury said Embraer should 'think twice' and called it 'a big risk'. Fortune (2024-05-04) said any Embraer narrowbody would likely enter service in the mid-to-late 2030s, and cited a 2024 BofA note welcoming the idea. Exact date of the Gomes Neto interview not shown.
findings.source_title: Embraer CEO Says Global Jet Market Has Room for More Boeing and Airbus Rivals (Air Data News)

findings.claim: Leeham (September 2026) reports the industry split on whether Embraer will launch an A320neo/737 MAX-class jet: some call it bet-the-company, others say Embraer's low debt could absorb a misstep, with the C Series as the cautionary tale.
findings.detail: Subscription article; only the introduction was visible. Separately, KAI and Embraer signed an MOU on 2026-07-28 to explore aerostructures R&D and manufacturing (FlightGlobal; Seoul Economic Daily). It is not a narrowbody programme. KAI already builds E2 wing parts.
findings.source_title: Will Embraer Go Big by Developing a Large Narrowbody Jet? (Leeham)

findings.claim: Richard Aboulafia has called Embraer 'such a natural' to build a third-player jet, while warning that a clean-sheet narrowbody carries the risk that broke a $10bn company (Bombardier).
findings.detail: Qualitative view only; no price quantification was found from Aboulafia/AeroDynamic. Attribution comes from a search summary over several pages; date not shown.
findings.source_title: Here's what it would take for Embraer to break the Boeing-Airbus duopoly (City AM)

findings.claim: An AirInsight post asked whether the price war would ease 'with the Airbus and Boeing success at killing the market for potential competitors, who were very quiet at Paris', which reads heavy discounting as entry deterrence.
findings.detail: Supports the idea that incumbents cut prices pre-emptively while entrants (CSeries, C919, MC-21) were still years from entry into service. Only the comment thread was visible; the date was not shown but context points to the early-to-mid 2010s.
findings.source_title: Will Airbus and Boeing end the price war? (AirInsight)

model_inputs.name: Duopoly single-aisle price-cost margin (Lerner index) before entry
model_inputs.basis: ACA-2 (14-17% markups, sometimes 3-5%); MG-1 (BCA 13.0% operating margin, 2018); MG-2 (Airbus commercial about 10.4%, 2025). Calibrates the Cournot/HHI arithmetic used below.

model_inputs.name: Market-average net price cut on new single-aisle deals once a credible third supplier is in service (Boeing has fps)
model_inputs.basis: My Cournot calibration: industry Lerner = HHI/elasticity, set to 15% at 50/50. An entrant at 10/20/30% share gives price falls of 2.9/4.7/5.5% (1.9-7.6% across Lerner 10-20%). Consistent with ACA-1 (3.7% price response to a 5% cost shock) and ACA-3 (rival prices move only a few percent after A380 entry). ITC (CS-5) found the CSeries unlikely to depress prices generally. High end allows a launch-period price war like PW-3 (net prices about 18% lower in 2011-14), partly averaged over uncontested deals. At base, an incumbent margin of 15% falls to about 10.5%: about 4.5 points, or roughly a third of unit profit.

research.summary: The evidence points to a modest market-wide price effect from a third credible single-aisle maker, but large cuts in the campaigns where it actually bids. Structural work (Irwin-Pavcnik) puts aircraft price-cost margins around 14-17%. It finds prices move only a few percent after shocks: +3.7% after the 1992 subsidy rules, and rivals' prices change little when an entrant product (the A380) arrives, which takes most from its closest substitutes. Calibrated Cournot arithmetic on those margins gives about a 3-6% fall in market-average net price when an entrant reaches 10-30% share, so 5% is the base. Calibrated models are known to be very sensitive to the 2-versus-3 firm question, so the band is wide (2-10%). Episodes show what happens in contested deals: Boeing cut about 45% below normal net pricing to keep the CS100 out of United (2016). Bombardier priced the CSeries about two-thirds off list and booked a $492M loss on 127 launch orders. The A220 went to JetBlue at 66-72% off against the E2. PROEX financing gave Embraer about a 13-15% price edge over the CRJ. The US ITC nevertheless found no injury to Boeing and no general price depression, and treated the Delta deal as a one-off. Pressure starts well before entry into service: the neo/MAX price war began at the 2010-11 launches, 5-6 years before entry into service, and incumbents discounted pre-emptively against entrants. But airlines commit to an entrant only when it is close to service, so I model the effect starting about 4 years before entry into service, half felt at entry into service and full about 3 years later. If Boeing has no new airplane, the cut is larger (base 1.3x) only if customers use the entrant to discipline Airbus. If the entrant simply replaces Boeing's MAX as the second source, the market price effect is about unchanged. In that case Airbus bears most of the per-unit price cut and Boeing most of the lost volume. Airline appetite is documented: in a BofA/Aviation Week survey, 71% would buy an Embraer narrowbody on merit, and United's Kirby and Ryanair's O'Leary both complain of duopoly leverage. But no sell-side house has published a quantified third-supplier price effect, and the C919 has shown no measurable effect on Western prices so far.

Caveat first: I could verify only 4 of 35 findings (A220-4, MG-1, MG-2 confirmed; RJ-3, PW-4 and CS-3 corrected from primary transcripts). The rest are unverifiable because the web was blocked. So most input bases rest on unchecked secondary claims.

(1) Lerner index 0.10/0.15/0.20. MG-1 (13.0%) and MG-2 (10.4%) are operating margins after R&D, SG&A and program-accounting averaging, not (p - mc)/p. ACA-2 is a wide-body 1969-98 estimate. The true single-aisle Lerner is probably above the operating margin. This input drives everything else, because in the Cournot formula the price cut scales with it. A 20% entrant gives -4.7% at L=0.15 but about -8.5% at L=0.25. Either widen the high end to 0.25-0.30, or set the market-average cut directly and vary it together with L in the sensitivity runs.

(2) Market-average cut 2%/5%/10%. The order of magnitude is defensible. ITC (unverified), Boeing's CFO in 2016 ('nothing material') and today's slot scarcity all argue for small market-wide effects. Airbus expects undersupply to persist, and Boeing reports 'better pricing environment... minimal slots'. Drop ACA-1 (cost pass-through) and ACA-3 (wide-body A380) from the basis; they are not entry effects. Do not use PW-3's 18% as an entrant case. That figure is a duopoly product-transition war. The game already has its own trigger for one, the Airbus NGSA and fps launches, so model it separately. Recommend making the cut depend on the backlog: damp it while incumbent backlogs exceed several years of output.

(3) Campaign-level cut 8%/15%/40%. The 40% high rests on CS-6 (unverified; an end-of-line 737-700 deal the ITC treated as one-off) and on launch-customer pricing (PW-2, PW-3), which is not an entrant contest. RJ-1 is a PROEX financing subsidy, not a price cut. Suggest low 0.05, base 0.10-0.15, high 0.25-0.30.

(4) Share of campaigns contested 0.15/0.3/0.5. Acceptable, but SUR-1 measures willingness to consider Embraer, not contest rate. Cap the implied wins by capacity. At 20 a month (240 a year) against roughly 1,500 or more incumbent single-aisle deliveries a year, the entrant can take only about 12-15% of units. The 30% share behind the high multiplier needs about 50 a month.

(5) Price pressure starts 2/4/6 years before entry into service. The basis is incumbent re-engine launches (neo/MAX), not entrant pressure. For the CSeries (launched 2008, entry into service 2016), the deep contested deals (United in January 2016, Delta in April 2016) came within about a year of entry into service, and Embraer called that competition 'short term'. Embraer's 2016 remark shows the earlier channel was an incumbent product response, not price. Suggest splitting the two: a product-response or launch-timing effect from 3-6 years before entry into service, and a price effect starting at low 0, base 2, high 4 years before.

(6) Share felt by entry into service 0.3/0.5/0.8. Fine. The CSeries record argues for a base nearer 0.3-0.4.

(7) No-fps multiplier 1.0/1.3/1.8. Logic is fine, but 1.8 assumes a 25-30% entrant share, which conflicts with 20 a month. Use about 1.5 as the high unless the entrant's rate grows.

(8)-(10) Airbus and Boeing split shares. These are analysis-only and plausible. A220-3 and C9-3 are unverified. Airbus's report confirms that the E2 overlaps the A220 and smallest A320neo, so an Embraer narrowbody would press on Airbus's A220/A320 range.

(11) Entrant price below own cost 0.15/0.3/0.5. Embraer's CEO says 'we don't sell our aircraft below cost' (May 2024), and Embraer runs a 2-3% commercial margin. CS-3's roughly 15-20% of price is Bombardier's and unverified. CS-2's 41% is an interested party's adjusted number. ACA-4's 50% is below learning-curve marginal cost at introduction, not below average cost. For an Embraer-led programme, suggest low 0, base about 0.10-0.15, high 0.30. research.summary: Partners have carried a real but limited share of airframers' development bills, and most of the money behind them came from their governments. Boeing's Japanese partners took 21% of the 777's airframe content and risk capital, with a state bank lending ¥60B to cover 60% of their part. On the 787 they took about 35% of the structure, sought state loans for 70% of their part, and were reported to get $1.6-2B of state support. On the A350, Airbus targeted €1.8B (about 16% of an €11B bill) from risk-sharing partners and about €3.2B (about 29%) from European governments. Embraer's 1990s model had outside partners and suppliers fund about 43%. Returns were poor for the weaker 787 partners: Boeing bought Vought's North Charleston plant for about $580M plus forgiven advances in 2009, bought out Alenia's half of Global Aeronautica, and Leonardo's aerostructures unit still lost €129M EBITA in the first nine months of 2024. The Boeing-Embraer deal ($4.2B for 80%, about $5.25B for 100%) was cancelled by Boeing in April 2020 and closed with a $150M payment to Embraer in September 2024. That walk-away is a trust cost any new Boeing-Embraer deal would carry. For the model, a partner share of the fps bill of 8% / 20% / 35% (about $5B / $12.5B / $22B) is evidenced. In return, partners would take about a pro-rata share of programme profit or more (1.0-1.5x). Expressed as a shipset premium, that is about $0.8M / $3.2M / $8.1M per aircraft (1.4% / 5.8% / 14.7% of $55M). The value to Boeing depends almost entirely on the partner's cost of capital. At a 7% hurdle against Boeing's 10.5% WACC, each $1 moved saves about $0.34 in PV. At a 10% hurdle it saves almost nothing, so state-backed partners (Japan, possibly Korea or Saudi Arabia) matter most. The partner candidates in track 4 (METI's 2035 plan, KAI, PIF, Tata, Leonardo, the UK, NASA's X-66A) and the Spirit buyback could not be researched because the search budget ran out. They remain open.

research.summary: Japan is the only Asian partner with a record of funding Boeing development with state backing. Japanese heavy-industry firms working through JADC took about 10% each on the 767, 21% of the 777's airframe content and risk capital, about 35% of the 787 structure and about 21% of the 777X structure. A state bank lent 60% of their 777 costs, and they sought loans for 70% of their 787 costs. Scaled to a $60-65B fps bill, that record points to a Japanese share of about 8% (range 4-15%). Korea's firms are smaller: KAI has about $2.6B of revenue, and Korean Air's aerospace division is smaller still. They already build parts for Boeing, Airbus and Embraer at the same time. Since July 2026 a state-led KASA task force, set up with KAI, Korean Air and Hanwha, has made a core risk-sharing role on the Airbus or Boeing next single-aisle (starting around 2030) Korea's main goal. That points to a Korean share of the fps bill of about 3% (range 1-8%). The Embraer track has backing from President Lee and a non-binding KAI-Embraer MoU signed on 28 July 2026, but Seoul calls it 'very early stage' and runs it alongside the main track. Boeing says a new airplane is 'not any time near' (CFO, March 2026). It also says the next airplane will use 'different kind of business partnerships, different type of ventures' to capture more value (CEO, July 2026). Since the 787 it has taken core IP, such as the 777X wing, back in-house, so offers to partners may be smaller or shaped as joint ventures. State-backed money is the main prize. At about 5.5% (Japan) or 7% (Korea) in dollar terms, against Boeing's 10.5%, each $1 of the bill moved to a partner saves Boeing about $0.45 or $0.34 in present value. Backing both Boeing and Embraer is normal at supplier level. The conflict comes with state-funded co-development of a direct rival, which would most likely cut Korea's fps role to build-to-print work (about 1%) rather than to zero. I put the chance that Korea commits to Embraer rather than Boeing at 25% (10-45%). It depends heavily on Boeing's timing: about 12% if Boeing launches the fps in 2030 and about 45% if Boeing has not launched by 2035. For Japan the chance is about 5%. findings.claim: Boeing shared the 767 with risk-sharing partners Aeritalia and Japan's Civil Transport Development Corporation (CTDC), with each partner's stake reported at about 10%, and repaid them with supply contracts.

findings.claim: On the 787, Mitsubishi, Kawasaki and Fuji were contracted through JADC for about 35% of the structure, with formal Boeing-JADC contracts signed in May 2005.
findings.detail: Several FlightGlobal and Asia Matters for America results agree on about 35%. A FlightGlobal headline ties the state development-bank loan to signing the 35% workshare contract. From an earlier run's search extract.

findings.claim: For the 787, JADC sought a state loan covering 70% of the Japanese partners' development costs, modelled on the 777 scheme. While the scheme was pending, the partners paid early costs from their own funds.
findings.detail: FlightGlobal: 'Fuji, Kawasaki and Mitsubishi were covering mounting development costs with internal funds because the Japanese government had not yet finalized a loan scheme for JADC.' The support took the form of loans, not grants, and the loans reportedly awaited airline launch orders. From an earlier run's search extract.
findings.source_title: FlightGlobal: Japanese 7E7 loans await airline launch orders

findings.claim: Estimates of Japanese state support for the heavies' 787 work range from about $1.6B (Seattle Times, 2005) to 'up to $2 billion in loans' (Asia Matters for America), and European officials called it an improper subsidy.
findings.detail: The Seattle Times (1 May 2005) said the government 'is expected to pump an estimated $1.6 billion into its companies' 787 work'. Implied Japanese 787 outlay: $1.6-2B divided by 0.7, about $2.3-2.9B in 2005 dollars (my arithmetic). Final drawn and repaid amounts were not found. From an earlier run's search extract.
findings.source_title: Seattle Times: Heavies help carry 787

findings.claim: Boeing and the Japanese partners signed a memorandum of agreement in June 2014 for about 21% of the 777X's major structure, followed by a formal agreement in July 2015.
findings.detail: Boeing's release says the value of parts bought from Japan will be proportionately higher than on the 777 because the 777X is larger. The 777X was launched in November 2013 (repo evidence BX-0057), so the MoA came about 7 months after launch and the formal contract about 20 months after. No figure was found for Japanese development funding or a state loan on the 777X. From an earlier run's search extract.
findings.source_title: Boeing: Boeing, Japanese Partners Reach Agreement on 777X Supplier Work

findings.claim: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries ended the SpaceJet on 7 February 2023 after about ¥1 trillion (about $7.6B) of development, without a single delivery.
findings.detail: MHI blamed an 'insufficient initial understanding of the complex type certification process' and a lack of money for long-term development. Losses included ¥263.3bn in FY2019 (including ¥122.4bn of impairment) and an ¥80.6bn impairment in FY2021. Japan's own-airliner attempt failed, which pushes Tokyo back towards partnering with a Western prime. From the franchise research run (franchise_research.json), WebSearch extracts.

findings.source_title: The Air Current on Embraer, Saudi Arabia/PIF and other funders

Also: 'It could require a little more vertical integration. I don't think a massive amount ... depending on the commodity, you're going to see different business relationships, different business models.' findings.detail: Jim Albaugh, 24 May 2011: 'one of the unintended consequences of all the outsourcing we did is we paid people to develop IP that they now own ... We want to control the critical IP.' Asked whether Boeing was working with 'the Spirits, and the Mitsubishis of the world' on their capital for a new narrowbody, Albaugh said the effort was 'for the most part, internal'. Read by me in the repository transcript (text page about 2606).

findings.detail: Ray Conner, 21 May 2014: 'we've already done a composite wing with Mitsubishi, and we were the ones that pretty much set up that production system there' ... 'having it in Everett ... significantly derisked the program.' Implication: on an fps Boeing is likely to keep the wing, which limits the size of a Japanese package unless the deal model changes. Read by me in the repository transcript (text page about 1983).

Competitor list: 'Airbus ... and other entrants from Russia, China and Japan' (FY2012-FY2020), then 'Airbus and entrants from China' (FY2022-FY2024), per the politics research run and the 10-K text I read. Repository Boeing 10-K compilation.

findings.claim: In 2016 Embraer said it would not launch an aircraft larger than the E2 while Boeing and Airbus remain in that segment, but would 'look again' if they moved up and left part of the market.
findings.detail: Paulo Cesar de Souza e Silva, FQ3 2016 call, 31 October 2016: 'we don't see a strong business case to compete head to head with Airbus and Boeing. So if they decide to move upwards ... and give up a little bit of this market, yes, at that moment, it's different.' Implication: Embraer's entry, and so Korea's Embraer option, is more likely if Boeing delays or skips the fps. Read by me in the repository Embraer transcripts (text page about 695).

findings.claim: Embraer said in 2011 that it would not accept any role as a sub-supplier or 'major risk-sharing partner' to another airframer and wants to stay independent with its own access to customers.
findings.detail: Frederico Curado, FQ4 2010 call, 25 March 2011, answering a question on a possible Boeing-Mitsubishi tie-up: 'we do not contemplate any architecture where Embraer will be a sub-supplier or sub-tier or tier-0.5 or a major risk-sharing partner.' Curado also said 'I don't see Boeing reacting going after Mitsubishi.' Implication: in an Embraer-Korea airliner, Embraer would lead and Korea would be a partner. Read by me in the repository Embraer transcripts (text page about 1092).

findings.claim: Airbus CEO Guillaume Faury said Airbus plans to choose an engine for its A320 successor in 2027, launch around 2030 and enter service in 2037 or 2038. Faury also said Embraer should 'think twice' before entering the narrowbody market.
findings.detail: Air Data News report dated 26 June 2026. Airbus will therefore be signing risk-sharing partners about when Korea's KASA programme targets 'Airbus/Boeing next-generation single-aisle' roles (KOR-1). Airbus, not Boeing, is the first prime able to take up Korea's and Japan's partner ambitions. KAI and Korean Air already build A320 and A350 parts (KOR-4, KOR-5). From an earlier run's search extract.
findings.source_title: Air Data News: Airbus CEO says Embraer should think twice before entering narrowbody market

findings.claim: Scaled to the whole fps bill, Japan's Boeing record implies a Japanese share of about 8% (range 4-15%), because its big percentages are shares of airframe structure, not of the whole programme bill.
findings.detail: 787: state support of $1.6-2B covering about 70% (JPN-5, JPN-6) implies Japanese outlay of about $2.3-2.9B in 2005 dollars. At an assumed 2.5% a year for about 30 years (x2.1), that is about $4.8-6.1B, or 7.7-9.8% of a $62.5B bill. A 777X-type package (21% of structure, wing kept by Boeing, JPN-7, BOE-4) gives the low end of about 4%. A larger co-developer role of the kind Ortberg hints at (BOE-1), plus Japan's post-SpaceJet push to partner (JPN-8), gives the high end of about 15%. This is my analysis.
findings.source_title: Analysis from JPN-2 to JPN-7, BOE-1, BOE-4

Korea base (3%, $1.9B at 7%): premium about $0.48M (0.9%), saving about 34%. Japan high (15% at 3.5%): about $1.53M, 58%. Korea high (8% at 5%): about $1.00M, 49%. findings.claim: A Korean commitment to Embraer would most likely shrink Korea's fps role to build-to-print work rather than end it, because Korean firms already supply Boeing, Airbus and Embraer at the same time. The conflict arises only for state-funded co-development of a direct competitor.
findings.detail: Today KAI builds for the 737NG, 777X, A320 and A350 and makes Embraer wing structures, and Korean Air builds 737-787 parts, A320neo sharklets and Embraer fuselage parts (KOR-4, KOR-5, KOR-11). What would clash: (a) money, since one airliner costs about 15 trillion won (KOR-3) and Korea's state-backed capacity is limited; (b) IP, since Boeing has learned to guard core IP from partners (BOE-3, BOE-4) and would be unlikely to give a core module to a firm co-developing a rival; (c) politics, since Korea's home airline has just ordered 50 737-10s (KOR-7) and KASA's stated main track is Airbus/Boeing (KOR-1). This is my analysis.
findings.source_title: Analysis from KOR-1, KOR-3, KOR-4, KOR-5, KOR-7, KOR-11, BOE-3, BOE-4

model_inputs.name: japan_partner_share_of_fps_bill
model_inputs.unit: fraction of the $60-65B fps development bill funded by Japanese partners (JADC heavies with state loans)
model_inputs.basis: ANL-1. Japanese partners took about 10% on the 767 (JPN-1), 21% of 777 airframe risk capital (JPN-2), about 35% of 787 structure (JPN-4) and about 21% of 777X structure (JPN-7). These are structure shares. Converted to dollars, the 787 package was about $2.3-2.9B (2005), about $4.8-6.1B in 2030s money, or 7.7-9.8% of $62.5B. Low: a 777X-type package with Boeing keeping the wing (BOE-4). High: a co-developer or joint-venture role (BOE-1) and Japan's post-SpaceJet appetite (JPN-8). The METI 2024 strategy could not be verified (see gaps).

model_inputs.name: japan_partner_funded_dollars
model_inputs.basis: The share above times the $62.5B midpoint bill.

model_inputs.name: japan_state_loan_cover_of_partner_own_cost
model_inputs.unit: fraction of the Japanese partners' own development cost lent by the state
model_inputs.basis: 777: ¥60B from a state bank covering 60% of JADC's costs, with interest initially covered (JPN-3). 787: JADC sought 70% (JPN-5). Low allows for post-2020 WTO pressure toward market terms (earlier run's AIR-A350-4) and Japan's budget.

model_inputs.name: korea_partner_share_of_fps_bill_if_korea_partners_boeing
model_inputs.unit: fraction of the fps development bill funded by Korean partners (KAI, Korean Air, Hanwha, with KASA/state backing)
model_inputs.basis: Korean firms are smaller than Japan's: KAI has about $2.6B of revenue, and its civil work is parts and panels for Boeing and Airbus (KOR-4, KOR-5). Korea wants core-module, risk-sharing roles on the Airbus/Boeing successors (KOR-1) and a 135 trillion won order target over 20 years from 2035 (KOR-2). It has sized a whole mid-size airliner at about 15 trillion won (KOR-3). In the Embraer case the earlier run put Korea at about 30% of a roughly $12B bill (about $3.6B). Base: about $1.9B, about a 777X-type Korean module. High: about $5B, if the state funds a full major module and Korea does not go with Embraer. Low: a build-to-print role with little risk capital.

model_inputs.name: korea_partner_share_of_fps_bill_if_korea_commits_to_embraer
model_inputs.unit: fraction of the fps development bill
model_inputs.basis: ANL-3. Supplier-level work for both rivals continues (KOR-11), but Boeing is unlikely to give a core module to a partner co-developing a direct rival (BOE-3, BOE-4), and Korean state money would be committed to Embraer (KOR-3).

model_inputs.name: japan_partner_cost_of_capital
model_inputs.basis: Blend of a state loan for 50-70% of the partner's cost (777 loan with interest initially covered, JPN-3; 787 sought 70%, JPN-5) and partner equity at a corporate hurdle. Converted to USD-equivalent because yen funding against dollar revenue carries currency risk. The high end allows for market-consistent state terms after the WTO cases. Derived; no Japanese partner hurdle rate was found. Against Boeing's 10.5% WACC, the base saves about $0.45 per $1 moved (ANL-2).

model_inputs.name: korea_partner_cost_of_capital
model_inputs.basis: Korean policy finance (KASA, Korea Eximbank, the presidential push, KOR-1/KOR-2) is likely to cover only part of the cost, with no proven Korean airliner-loan scheme like Japan's. KAI and Hanwha carry corporate hurdles nearer Boeing's. Derived; no sourced rate. Base saves about $0.34 per $1 moved; high about $0.16; low about $0.49 (ANL-2).

model_inputs.name: p_korea_commits_to_embraer_rather_than_boeing
model_inputs.unit: probability (0-1), Korea's lead state-backed co-development commitment goes to an Embraer airliner rather than to the Boeing fps, over the 2030-2035 decision rounds
model_inputs.basis: Against: KASA's official main track is the Airbus/Boeing successors (KOR-1); the Embraer talks are 'very early stage' (KOR-9) and the MoU is non-binding (KOR-10); Korean Air has just ordered 50 737-10s (KOR-7); and Embraer has no programme and will define products only from 2030 (earlier run, r_embkor). For: presidential-level priority on two visits (KOR-8, KOR-13); KAI wants a risk-sharing co-developer role it cannot get as a Boeing tier-1 (KOR-11); Aviation Week calls Brazil the leading candidate (KOR-12); and Boeing says a launch is 'not any time near' (BOE-2). The earlier run put the chance of an Embraer-Korea launch by 2032 at 35%, and this probability should stay below that. My judgement.

model_inputs.name: p_korea_commits_to_embraer_if_boeing_launches_fps_2030
model_inputs.basis: A 2030 Boeing launch, plus Airbus launching around 2030 (AIR-1), would give Korea two prime offers at once and fill KASA's main track (KOR-1). Embraer has said it will not go bigger while both incumbents stay in the segment (EMB-A). My judgement.

model_inputs.name: p_korea_commits_to_embraer_if_no_boeing_launch_by_2035
model_inputs.basis: If Boeing stalls, Embraer's own stated condition (incumbents leaving part of the market, EMB-A) moves closer, Korea's presidential push has no Boeing outlet, and only Airbus is left as a prime alternative. Limited by Embraer's caution and its need for a mature engine (earlier run). My judgement.

model_inputs.name: p_japan_backs_embraer_rather_than_boeing
model_inputs.basis: There is only one unnamed-source report of Embraer-Japan talks (JPN-9). Against it: four decades of JADC programme partnership with Boeing (JPN-1 to JPN-7), Japan's 100-aircraft Boeing trade commitment (JPN-10) and the SpaceJet loss (JPN-8). The high end allows Japan to hedge if Boeing offers only a small package (BOE-4) or keeps delaying (BOE-2).

model_inputs.name: p_japan_takes_fps_risk_sharing_package_if_boeing_launches
model_inputs.basis: Japan took risk-sharing packages on the 767, 777, 787 and 777X (JPN-1 to JPN-7). Downside risks: Boeing's move toward keeping core work and value (BOE-1, BOE-3, BOE-4), the Airbus NGSA courting the same partners first (AIR-1), and the fact that no Japanese single-aisle package precedent was found. My judgement.

model_inputs.name: lag_from_fps_launch_to_partner_funding_agreement
model_inputs.basis: 777X: launched November 2013 (repo BX-0057), Japanese MoA June 2014 (about 0.6 years), formal agreement July 2015 (about 1.7 years) (JPN-7). 787: Japanese partners paid early costs internally until the state loan scheme and the May 2005 contracts were in place (JPN-4, JPN-5). So partner money arrives after the launch decision, and Boeing carries the early years.
